Your understanding is almost completely correct. Let me refine it a bit.

How GSoC actually works

Plain text
January │ ├── Organizations apply to Google │ February │ ├── Google announces accepted organizations ├── Organizations publish project ideas ├── Contributors start talking with mentors ├── Contributors START CONTRIBUTING (this is important) │ March │ ├── Contributor application opens ├── You submit your proposal(s) │ April │ ├── Organizations review proposals ├── Accepted contributors announced │ May │ ├── Community Bonding (about 3 weeks) │ ├── Learn the codebase │ ├── Meet mentor │ ├── Finalize milestones │ May → August │ ├── Coding Period │ ├── Midterm Evaluation │ └── Final Evaluation

The biggest misconception many first-time applicants have is:

They think GSoC starts when applications open.

It doesn't.

For successful applicants, GSoC usually starts 3–6 months before the application deadline. They spend that time getting to know the organization, making contributions, and building trust. Organizations strongly encourage early interaction with mentors and contributions before submitting a proposal. Google Summer of Code+1

Your situation

You said:

I have never done Open Source.

That's completely fine.

Most successful GSoC contributors started exactly there.

The difference is that they prepared before GSoC.

Before Open Source, what do you need to know?

There are two categories.

1. Technical Skills

You already have most of these.

✅ Git (basic)

✅ GitHub

✅ JavaScript / TypeScript

✅ React

✅ Node

✅ Python

✅ Docker

✅ PostgreSQL

✅ Reading documentation

You're already much stronger than many first-time applicants in terms of programming.

2. Open Source Workflow

This is what you need to learn.

Git

Not just commits.

You should know

  • clone
  • branch
  • checkout
  • merge
  • rebase (basic understanding)
  • stash
  • cherry-pick (optional)
  • resolving merge conflicts

GitHub

You should understand

  • Fork
  • Clone
  • Upstream
  • Origin
  • Pull Request
  • Review comments
  • Discussions
  • Issues
  • Labels
  • Milestones
  • Draft PR
  • Code Owners

Repository Structure

When opening a repository, you should know where to look.

Code
README.md CONTRIBUTING.md CODE_OF_CONDUCT.md LICENSE docs/ src/ tests/ .github/

Reading Existing Code

This is probably the biggest skill.

Open source is not:

I write code.

It is:

I understand someone else's code and improve it.

You need to learn

  • navigating a codebase
  • tracing function calls
  • understanding architecture
  • finding where features live

Issues

Every organization uses issues.

Learn

Code
Good First Issue Help Wanted Bug Feature Enhancement Discussion

Pull Requests

You'll eventually make many PRs.

Workflow:

Code
Issue ↓ Fork ↓ Create Branch ↓ Code ↓ Commit ↓ Push ↓ Open PR ↓ Mentor Reviews ↓ Changes Requested ↓ Update PR ↓ Merged

Code Reviews

Probably the most important thing.

Maintainers might say:

Rename this variable.

This function is too long.

Follow project style.

Write tests.

You shouldn't take review comments personally—they're a normal part of collaborative development.

Documentation

Read lots of documentation.

Examples:

  • README
  • API docs
  • Contribution guide
  • Architecture docs

Communication

This is surprisingly important.

Organizations communicate through

  • GitHub Discussions
  • Discord
  • Slack
  • Matrix
  • Mailing Lists

You need to learn professional communication.

Debugging

Open source involves fixing existing software.

You should be comfortable with

  • reading logs
  • reproducing bugs
  • using breakpoints
  • browser DevTools
  • inspecting stack traces

Testing

Know how to

  • run tests
  • write basic tests
  • fix failing tests

What does a beginner actually do?

Usually:

Code
Fix typo ↓ Improve documentation ↓ Small UI bug ↓ Simple backend bug ↓ Small feature ↓ Medium feature ↓ Large feature ↓ GSoC proposal

No one starts by implementing a huge feature.

How should YOU start?

Knowing your background (React, Node, TypeScript, FastAPI, Docker, PostgreSQL, AI projects), here's the path I'd recommend.

Phase 1 (1 week)

Learn Git properly.

Understand

  • branches
  • pull requests
  • merge conflicts
  • forks

Phase 2 (1 week)

Learn GitHub workflow.

Practice on your own repositories:

  • create issues
  • create branches
  • open pull requests
  • review changes

Phase 3 (2 weeks)

Contribute to small repositories.

Not GSoC yet.

Just learn.

Examples:

  • documentation fixes
  • typo fixes
  • README improvements

Phase 4 (2–3 weeks)

Choose one recurring GSoC organization.

Examples:

  • Apache
  • FOSSASIA
  • Django
  • OWASP

Read everything:

  • README
  • CONTRIBUTING
  • Issues
  • Discussions
  • Project Ideas

Do not start coding immediately.

Phase 5

Start solving

  • Good First Issues
  • Beginner Issues
  • Documentation Issues

Get your first merged PR.

Then your second.

Then your third.

Only after a few successful contributions should you start thinking about your GSoC proposal.

Your biggest advantage

Compared to many first-time GSoC applicants, you're already comfortable building complete applications:

  • React
  • Node.js
  • FastAPI
  • PostgreSQL
  • Docker
  • Redis
  • ML integration

That means your main challenge is not coding—it's learning how to collaborate in an established codebase and community.

What I would do if I were preparing you for GSoC 2027

I'd structure it like a roadmap:

  • Stage 1: Master Git & GitHub workflows.
  • Stage 2: Make 10–15 small open-source contributions across different repositories.
  • Stage 3: Select 2–3 recurring GSoC organizations that align with your interests.
  • Stage 4: Become an active contributor in one organization by fixing bugs, discussing issues, and interacting with mentors.
  • Stage 5: Write a strong proposal based on work you've already done in that organization.

This approach gives you real experience before the application period and significantly improves your chances compared to applying with only a proposal.

Time: 5–7 days.

Level 2 — GitHub (Remote Collaboration)

GitHub is where collaboration happens.

You'll learn concepts such as:

  • Repository
  • Fork
  • Clone
  • Remote
  • Origin
  • Upstream
  • Pull Request (PR)
  • Review
  • Merge
  • GitHub Issues
  • Labels
  • Milestones
  • Projects
  • Discussions
  • Releases
  • Stars
  • Watch
  • CODEOWNERS
  • Branch Protection

This is where you'll start to understand how a project is organized.

Time: 4–5 days.

Level 3 — Open Source Workflow

This is the part that connects Git and GitHub into a real contribution.

A typical workflow looks like this:

Plain text
Maintainer creates Issue ↓ You choose an Issue ↓ Comment that you'd like to work on it ↓ Fork the repository ↓ Clone your fork ↓ Create a new branch ↓ Write code ↓ Commit changes ↓ Push to your fork ↓ Open a Pull Request ↓ Maintainer reviews your code ↓ You make requested changes ↓ PR is merged

If you understand this flow, you've understood the heart of open source.

Time: 3–4 days.

Level 4 — Community

Now you learn the human side.

Things like:

  • How to ask questions
  • How to report bugs
  • How to communicate with maintainers
  • How to respond to review comments
  • Writing good commit messages
  • Writing good issue descriptions
  • Writing good PR descriptions

Time: 2–3 days.

Total time

If you're studying 1.5–2 hours every day:

StageTime
Git1 week
GitHub1 week
Open Source Workflow4–5 days
Community Practices3–4 days

So in about 3 weeks, you can become comfortable with the workflow itself.

Notice I didn't say "master." Mastery comes only after making real contributions, but in three weeks you'll understand how everything fits together.

What you should know about each GitHub term

Here's a preview of the concepts you'll eventually master.

ConceptSimple meaning
RepositoryThe project folder containing the code and history.
ForkYour own copy of someone else's repository under your GitHub account.
CloneDownload a repository from GitHub to your computer.
BranchAn isolated line of development so you don't affect the main code.
CommitA saved snapshot of your changes.
PushUpload your commits to GitHub.
PullDownload the latest changes from GitHub.
Pull RequestA request asking maintainers to merge your changes into their project.
IssueA task, bug report, feature request, or discussion topic.
LabelsTags that categorize issues and PRs (e.g., bug, good first issue).
MilestoneA collection of issues grouped toward a release or goal.
ReviewFeedback on your pull request from maintainers.
MergeCombining your branch into another branch (usually main).
UpstreamThe original repository you forked from.
OriginYour own fork or the remote repository linked to your local clone.

By the end of your learning, each of these should feel as natural as terms like "function" or "API."

How I would teach you

Instead of watching random YouTube videos, I'd recommend treating this like a short course.

Week 1 – Git Fundamentals

  • Learn Git concepts and commands.
  • Practice entirely on local repositories.

Week 2 – GitHub Collaboration

  • Create repositories.
  • Fork projects.
  • Clone repositories.
  • Create branches.
  • Push changes.
  • Open pull requests.
  • Learn issues and labels.

Week 3 – Simulated Open Source

We'll create a mock open source project and simulate everything:

  • An issue is created.
  • You assign it to yourself.
  • You create a branch.
  • You fix the problem.
  • You commit.
  • You push.
  • You open a pull request.
  • I review it as if I were the maintainer.
  • You update the PR based on review comments.
  • The PR gets merged.

After doing this a few times, the workflow becomes second nature.

I actually think this is the best path for you because it separates learning the collaboration process from contributing to real projects. Once the workflow is second nature, you can focus entirely on understanding code and making meaningful contributions instead of wondering what a fork or a pull request is. Based on what I know about your background, this foundational phase should take you around 3–4 weeks, after which you'll be ready to start contributing to beginner-friendly open source repositories with confidence.

What organizations actually care about

Many students think:

That's usually not why proposals get rejected.

  • Can this person understand our codebase?
  • Can they communicate well?
  • Will they respond to review comments?
  • Can they complete what they promise?
  • Have they already contributed?

The proposal is almost like a job interview. Your prior contributions build trust.

In open source, you'll think:
